screens.title: Setting Up Your Ethereum Development Environment
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will prepare a repeatable development environment that lets you write, test, and deploy Solidity contracts quickly. We'll establish Node. js and npm as the foundation, scaffold a Hardhat project, and add the libraries and plugins you need to compile and test code in a local blockchain. You will also learn how to run Hardhat Network for rapid iterations and how to protect secrets like private keys. A practical example you will follow is creating a new project folder, running npm init to create package. json, installing Hardhat, and running npx hardhat to scaffold sample contracts and scripts. This setup matters because a consistent environment speeds debugging and testing and avoids common mistakes like missing plugins or misconfigured compiler versions. At the end of the chapter you will be able to start a local node, deploy a sample contract to it, and run tests — all without touching a public testnet. Notice common pitfalls as you go, such as forgetting to run the initialization command or accidentally committing secrets. As you work through the hands-on steps, ask yourself: does my project scaffold include contracts, scripts, tests, and a clear hardhat. config. js? That question will guide a resilient setup.

Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › Setting Up Your Environment
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Set up Node, npm and Hardhat

Create a dependable local toolchain using Node and npm, scaffold a Hardhat project, add ethers.js and testing plugins, and run a local Hardhat Network for fast, isolated testing.

In this lesson
From installation to local deployment: a practical, repeatable setup.
Prerequisite
A recent LTS of Node.js installed and terminal familiarity. Verify with the terminal commands shown.
Outcome
A scaffolded Hardhat project with plugins configured and a local node ready for deploys and tests.
Concept Map
Node & npm
Install and verify versions with the terminal.
Hardhat
Scaffolds projects, runs a local network, and integrates plugins.
ethers.js & Tests
Libraries for interacting with contracts and asserting behavior in tests.
Explore Key Topics
Install & Verify — Check node -v and npm -v to confirm your runtime.
Scaffold — Run npx hardhat to create contracts, scripts, and tests.
Local Node — Use npx hardhat node, then deploy to localhost for rapid feedback.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus your practice so you build a repeatable workflow for Ethereum development. First, you will install Node. js and npm and verify the installation with simple terminal commands. This ensures you can run JavaScript tooling and manage packages. Second, you will initialize a new Hardhat project using npx hardhat, which scaffolds a project with contracts, scripts, and tests; this step saves you from manual configuration and creates defaults you can extend. Third, you will explore the Hardhat project layout and learn what files like package. json and hardhat. config. js do; understanding these files reduces configuration errors later. Fourth, you will add essential plugins such as ethers. js and testing helpers, and learn why these libraries help with signing transactions, interacting with contracts, and asserting behavior in tests. Each objective pairs a practical command or file with why it matters in a real workflow, so you leave with skills you can repeat in any new project.

screens.title: Node.js and npm: Foundation of the Toolchain
screens.narratorSegment: Node. js is the JavaScript runtime that allows tools in this course to run on your machine outside of a browser. npm is the package manager bundled with Node that installs libraries, frameworks, and command-line tools. Together they make it possible to install Hardhat, ethers. js, and testing helpers and run scripts that compile, deploy, and test contracts. A concrete example is running node -v and npm -v in your terminal. If those commands return version numbers, your environment can run the tooling used in this course. A common misconception is that Node is only for web servers; in this context, it is the runtime that powers build tools, script runners, and test frameworks. Another mistake is installing an unsupported or very old Node version; prefer recent LTS releases to avoid compatibility issues with modern packages. Key takeaway: verify Node and npm first, because every other step depends on them. If a command fails, check your PATH and reinstall Node from a trusted installer. Reflect: can your machine run a simple npm package script and report its version? If yes, you have the foundation.

keyIdea.title: Why Node & npm
keyIdea.text: They run development scripts and manage dependencies; verifying them prevents downstream installation and runtime errors.

content.html:
Definition

Node.js and npm

Node.js executes JavaScript on your machine, while npm installs and manages packages. These tools let you install and run Hardhat, ethers.js, and test frameworks.

Verification example
node -v
npm -v
If these return versions, proceed. If not, install or reconfigure Node.
Why it matters
  • Hardhat and many libraries are distributed as npm packages; npm installs them into node_modules.
  • Build scripts, deployments, and tests are run with Node, so a working runtime is essential.
  • Package versions affect compatibility; prefer recent LTS releases of Node to avoid install errors.
Common mistake
Using an outdated Node version can cause install failures or runtime errors with modern packages.
Key Takeaway

Verify Node and npm first. They are the bedrock for everything that follows.

screens.title: Create and Initialize a Project
screens.narratorSegment: Starting a project is a small process with big benefits when it's done correctly. First, create an empty directory with a meaningful name and change into it. Next run npm init -y to generate a package. json file — this file records project metadata and the dependencies you will later install. The package. json is important because it makes your project reproducible on another machine; installing dependencies from package. json recreates the environment. A concrete example is creating my-first-hardhat-project, running npm init -y, then installing Hardhat as a development dependency. A common misconception is that npm init is optional; while you can install packages without it, having package. json simplifies dependency management, scripts, and version control. Also avoid manually editing important fields without understanding them; use npm set-script or your editor to update scripts instead. Key takeaway: initialize npm early so your project has a manifest and dependency tracking from day one, which reduces friction later when you add Hardhat and testing libraries. Create and Initialize a Project means npm init creates package.json which records dependencies and scripts, making your project reproducible and manageable.. In practical terms, directory creation, npm init, and why package.json matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Project Manifest
keyIdea.text: npm init creates package.json which records dependencies and scripts, making your project reproducible and manageable.

content.html:
Process

Initialize a Node project

Follow a small set of commands to create a project and a package.json manifest that tracks dependencies and scripts.

mkdir my-first-hardhat-project
cd my-first-hardhat-project
npm init -y
The -y flag accepts defaults so you get a package.json quickly.
Why: package.json makes installs repeatable and supports scripts.
Tip: name the directory clearly to reflect the project.
Practical example

After npm init -y, install Hardhat so you have the dev toolchain recorded as a devDependency.

npm install --save-dev hardhat
Installing as a dev dependency keeps production bundles clean.
Key Takeaway

Initialize npm early and record devDependencies so your environment can be reproduced across machines.

screens.title: Hardhat: The Development Framework
screens.narratorSegment: Hardhat is a flexible environment for compiling, testing, deploying, and debugging Solidity contracts. It bundles a task runner, plugin system, and a built-in local blockchain called Hardhat Network. The practical value is that it creates a consistent developer experience: you run standard tasks to compile, run tests, and deploy without manually wiring toolchains. A concrete example is running npx hardhat after installing the package; the command scaffolds a project and offers starter contracts and scripts. A common misconception is to treat Hardhat as only a compiler; in fact, it is an entire workflow that integrates testing libraries and blockchain simulation. Another mistake is installing the package but forgetting to run npx hardhat to create the starter files; this leaves a directory with node_modules and package. json but no contracts or scripts. Key takeaway: install Hardhat as a dev dependency and run its initializer to get a ready-to-use local environment that accelerates development and testing. Hardhat: The Development Framework means hardhat scaffolds projects, runs a local node, and integrates plugins to provide a full development workflow for solidity.. In practical terms, what hardhat provides and why it's chosen for this course. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Hardhat Role
keyIdea.text: Hardhat scaffolds projects, runs a local node, and integrates plugins to provide a full development workflow for Solidity.

content.html:
Core Concept

Hardhat provides an integrated workflow

It compiles contracts, runs tests, and provides a local network for deploying and debugging without a public testnet.

Starter command
npx hardhat
Running the initializer creates contracts, scripts, and test folders you can extend.
Practical benefits
  • Fast local iteration using Hardhat Network that resets between runs.
  • Plugin system to add ethers.js, testing matchers, and network helpers.
  • Starter sample contracts and deployment scripts for learning workflows.
Misconception
Installing Hardhat without running the initializer leaves no scaffolded files; always run npx hardhat after install.
Key Takeaway

Hardhat is more than a compiler; it is the workflow backbone for local Solidity development.

screens.title: Hardhat Project Structure
screens.narratorSegment: When you run the Hardhat initializer, it creates a predictable project layout: a hardhat. config. js file, a contracts folder for Solidity files, scripts for deployment or interaction, and a test folder for your automated tests. The hardhat. config. js file sets the Solidity compiler version, plugin requires, and network settings; it is the single place where your project’s behavior is configured. A concrete example is seeing Lock. sol in contracts and a deploy script in scripts when you choose the sample project; these give you a working end-to-end path from compilation to deployment. A common mistake is editing hardhat. config. js to include sensitive data like private keys directly; instead use environment variables and a. env file excluded from version control. Key takeaway: learn the role of each folder and the config file early; this reduces time spent searching for where to change compiler versions, add plugin requires, or define networks for later deployments. keyIdea.title: Project Layout
keyIdea.text: Recognize contracts, scripts, tests, and hardhat.config.js so you can configure compilation, networks, and plugins effectively.

content.html:
Hierarchy

Typical scaffolded files and folders

  • hardhat.config.js — main configuration for compiler and plugins.
  • contracts/ — Solidity smart contract files like Greeter.sol or Lock.sol.
  • scripts/ — JavaScript deployment or interaction scripts.
  • test/ — test files using the installed testing framework.
Mnemonic: config + code + scripts + tests.
Concrete example
// hardhat.config.js (excerpt)
require("@nomicfoundation/hardhat-ethers");
/** @type import('hardhat/config').HardhatUserConfig */
module.exports = { solidity: "0.8.20" };
This example sets the compiler and includes the ethers plugin.
Misconception
Editing the config without understanding plugin requires can break tasks; add plugin requires at the top as shown by examples.
Key Takeaway

Familiarize yourself with the scaffolded folders and the config file; they are the control center for your project.

screens.title: Essential Plugins and Libraries
screens.narratorSegment: Hardhat supports plugins that extend its capabilities. The essential packages for this course include ethers. js for creating transactions and interacting with deployed contracts, and testing helpers such as chai matchers and network helpers for writing expressive tests. Modern plugin packages live under the @nomicfoundation scope and replace older hardhat-waffle integrations. A concrete install sequence installs the ethers integration and testing matchers together with chai and ethers. A common misconception is that these packages are optional; without them you lack a robust, convenient A P I for signing transactions and asserting contract behavior, which makes tests harder to write. When you add these packages, remember to require them in hardhat. config. js so tasks and tests can use them. Key takeaway: install and require the core plugins early so your scripts and tests can rely on a consistent A P I when interacting with contracts. keyIdea.title: Plugins
keyIdea.text: Install ethers.js and the testing matchers to interact with contracts and write robust tests; require them in hardhat.config.js.

content.html:
Install

Core packages to add

npm install --save-dev @nomicfoundation/hardhat-ethers@^3.0.0 
@nomicfoundation/hardhat-chai-matchers@^2.0.0 
@nomicfoundation/hardhat-network-helpers@^1.0.0 
chai ethers@^6.0.0
These modern packages replace older plugin names and provide integrated APIs.
Why each matters
  • ethers.js: high-quality library to sign and send transactions.
  • Chai & matchers: expressive assertions for contract behavior.
  • Network helpers: utilities to manage snapshots and time in tests.
Misconception
Installing the packages without requiring them in the config means tests won't load plugin features automatically.
Key Takeaway

Install and require these libraries so your scripts and tests can use a consistent API for blockchain interactions and assertions.

screens.title: Requiring Plugins and Configuring Hardhat
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring Hardhat is a simple but critical step. At the top of hardhat. config. js you add require statements for the plugins you installed so Hardhat loads their features. Then you export a configuration object that sets the Solidity compiler version and any network settings. A concrete example used in this chapter shows require calls for the ethers plugin, chai matchers, and network helpers followed by module. exports setting solidity to a recent version. A common mistake is to hardcode private keys or other secrets directly in this file. Instead, use environment variables and reference process environment values from the config. This practice keeps secrets out of version control. Key takeaway: require your plugins in hardhat. config. js and set the compiler version explicitly. Doing so makes builds reproducible and avoids silent test failures caused by compiler mismatches. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Config Example
keyIdea.text: Add plugin require statements and set a Solidity version in hardhat.config.js; use env variables for secrets instead of hardcoding.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough

hardhat.config.js (example)

require("@nomicfoundation/hardhat-ethers");
require("@nomicfoundation/hardhat-chai-matchers");
require("@nomicfoundation/hardhat-network-helpers");

/** @type import('hardhat/config').HardhatUserConfig */
module.exports = {
  solidity: "0.8.20",
  networks: {
    // network configs go here
  }
};
Why: require statements load plugin features available to tasks and tests.
Safety: avoid hardcoding private keys; read them from process.env in production-like configs.
Key Takeaway

Require plugins and set compiler versions in hardhat.config.js. Use environment variables to protect secrets.

screens.title: Hardhat Network Explained
screens.narratorSegment: Hardhat Network is a local Ethereum node built into Hardhat for development and testing. It runs locally in your terminal when you run Hardhat tasks and can also be explicitly started with npx hardhat node. The value of using Hardhat Network is speed and isolation: it resets state between runs so tests start with a clean slate, and it provides pre-funded accounts so you don't need to use public testnets for early development. A concrete example is starting the node and seeing a list of 20 test accounts, each pre-funded with a large test balance for experiments. A common misconception is that development on a local network is identical to public testnets; behavior can differ due to network and gas realities, so the local network is ideal for fast iteration but not a final integration test. screens.title: Common Setup Issues and How to Fix Them
screens.narratorSegment: Setting up a development environment often hits a small set of recurring problems. First, version mismatches: using an older Node version can cause installs to fail or binaries to behave unexpectedly. The fix is to verify node -v and npm -v and upgrade if necessary. Second, forgetting to run npx hardhat after installation leaves only node_modules and package. json without contracts or scripts; rerun the initializer to scaffold missing files. Third, typos in npm install commands or package names lead to missing plugins and runtime errors; re-run install with the correct package names and check package. json dependencies. Fourth, a common security error is hardcoding private keys in the config; the remedy is to use environment variables and. env files excluded from version control. A useful habit is reading terminal output carefully: error messages often point directly to the missing dependency or misconfiguration. Issue

Version mismatch or missing node

If npm install fails or binaries are missing, check versions with node -v and npm -v and reinstall or update Node to a recent LTS.

Fix
Upgrade Node or reinstall so the runtime supports modern packages.
Issue

Scaffold missing after install

If contracts, scripts, and tests are absent, you likely forgot to run the initializer after installing Hardhat.

Fix
Run npx hardhat and follow prompts to create a JavaScript project and starter files.
Issue

Plugin or test errors

Missing or incorrectly installed plugins cause tests to fail or features to be unavailable.

Fix
Reinstall the correct packages and add require statements in hardhat.config.js so plugins are loaded.
Issue

Secrets in config

Hardcoding private keys in hardhat.config.js risks exposing credentials if files are committed to version control.

Fix
Use environment variables, reference process.env, and keep .env in .gitignore.
Key Takeaway

Read terminal messages closely, verify versions, and follow safe config practices to avoid common setup pitfalls.

In this chapter you will prepare a repeatable development environment that lets you write, test, and deploy Solidity contracts quickly. We'll establish Node. js and npm as the foundation, scaffold a Hardhat project, and add the libraries and plugins you need to compile and test code in a local blockchain. You will also learn how to run Hardhat Network for rapid iterations and how to protect secrets like private keys. A practical example you will follow is creating a new project folder, running npm init to create package. json, installing Hardhat, and running npx hardhat to scaffold sample contracts and scripts. Setting up a development environment often hits a small set of recurring problems. First, version mismatches: using an older Node version can cause installs to fail or binaries to behave unexpectedly. The fix is to verify node -v and npm -v and upgrade if necessary. Second, forgetting to run npx hardhat after installation leaves only node_modules and package. json without contracts or scripts; rerun the initializer to scaffold missing files. Third, typos in npm install commands or package names lead to missing plugins and runtime errors; re-run install with the correct package names and check package. json dependencies. Fourth, a common security error is hardcoding private keys in the config; the remedy is to use environment variables and. env files excluded from version control. A useful habit is reading terminal output carefully: error messages often point directly to the missing dependency or misconfiguration. Key takeaway: verify versions, re-run the initializer if scaffold files are missing, correct typos, and never place secrets in committed config files. These concise concept cards summarize the most important ideas you should remember. Keep these three concepts in your mental toolbox: the runtime, the manifest, and the framework.
